extraction_notes.note: Two remark environments that only introduce notation (ordinary Lagrange density/tension field; pseudoharmonic equation and sections) were retyped as definitions.
Proposition introduced as 'an easy adaptation of a result due to Wood' with no proof: marked origin external (adapted) rather than a paper result with semi_formal rigor.

The Proposition on the isomorphism type of Theta and Psi 'follows from the previous discussion'; that discussion plus the computational remark was taken as its prose proof, the remark nested in the proof's last step.
The two italic statements in the introduction (points A and B) were emitted as main claims; the conclusions' restatements are kept in also_stated_at.

Most of the paper is definitional prose with many unproved one-sentence assertions ('it is easy to see', 'clearly'); these were emitted as claims with rigor semi_formal, and only arguments preceding a stated result were made proof nodes.

The Lie-bracket computation of the curvature in Appendix B.4, the remaining intermediate coordinate identities of Appendix B, and the research directions of Section 7 (gauging, other dimensions, deformation problems) were not made separate nodes.
The source has typos that affect symbols (e.g. 'tension filed', the pull-back of the fundamental bundle form written as Phi^s at the end of Section 4.4); the latter sentence was not extracted.

nodes.name: Supersymmetrization of GESM theories
nodes.statement:
The supersymmetrization of the
theories introduced in this paper is currently an open problem
involving several objects and structures of mathematical interest,
such as spinor bundles and Lipschitz structures, Special-K\"ahler and
Quaternionic-K\"ahler manifolds or exceptional Lie groups, all
interacting in a delicate equilibrium dictated by supersymmetry.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
also_stated_at:
First, it is natural to consider the supersymmetrization of
our theories.

nodes.name: GESM solutions as classical locally-geometric U-folds (integrable case)
nodes.statement:
When the Kaluza-Klein space is integrable, global
  solutions of the GESM theory correspond to classical
  locally-geometric U-folds glued from local solutions of the ordinary
  sigma model coupled to Abelian gauge fields (which may have a
  non-trivial duality structure) using symmetries of the equations of
  motion of the latter.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
assumptions: When the Kaluza-Klein space is integrable
conclusions:
global
  solutions of the GESM theory correspond to classical
  locally-geometric U-folds glued from local solutions of the ordinary
  sigma model coupled to Abelian gauge fields (which may have a
  non-trivial duality structure) using symmetries of the equations of
  motion of the latter
also_stated_at:
When the Kaluza-Klein space is integrable, we showed that the
  GESM theory is {\em locally indistinguishable} from the generalized
  ESM theory of \cite{GESM} and that its global solutions correspond
  to {\em classical} locally-geometric U-folds. This can be viewed as
  a rigorous mathematical definition of classical locally-geometric
  U-folds with scalar and Abelian gauge fields in the language of
  global differential geometry.
nodes.statement_short: In the integrable case, global GESM solutions are classical locally-geometric U-folds glued from local ESM solutions by duality symmetries.

nodes.name: GESM solutions glued from modified sigma models (non-integrable case)
nodes.statement:
When the Kaluza-Klein space is not integrable,
global solutions of the GESM theory can be glued from local solutions
of the modified sigma model coupled to Abelian gauge fields (which may
have a non-trivial duality structure).
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
assumptions: When the Kaluza-Klein space is not integrable
conclusions:
global solutions of the GESM theory can be glued from local solutions
of the modified sigma model coupled to Abelian gauge fields (which may
have a non-trivial duality structure)
also_stated_at:
When the Kaluza-Klein space is not integrable, we showed that
  GESM theories are locally equivalent with modified sigma models
  of maps into the fiber coupled to Abelian gauge fields, which
  differ {\em locally} from ordinary ESM theories.

nodes.name: Smoothness conventions
nodes.statement:
All manifolds considered are smooth, connected, Hausdorff and
paracompact (hence also second countable) while all fiber bundles
considered are smooth.
nodes.section: 1.1 Notations and conventions

nodes.name: Submersions surjective with connected fibers
nodes.statement:
All submersions considered are assumed to be
surjective and to have connected fibers.

nodes.name: Hom and Isom bundles
nodes.statement:
Given vector bundles $\mathcal{S}$
and $\mathcal{S}'$ over some manifold $M$, we denote by $Hom(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}')$,
$Isom(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}')$ the bundles of morphisms and isomorphisms from $\mathcal{S}$
to $\mathcal{S}'$ and by ${\rm Hom}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}')\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \Gamma(M, Hom(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}'))$,
$\mathrm{Isom}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}')\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \Gamma(M, Isom(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}'))$ the sets of smooth
sections of these bundles.

nodes.name: Pull-back bundle
nodes.statement:
Given a smooth map
$f:M_1\rightarrow M_2$ and a vector bundle $\mathcal{S}$ on $M_2$, we denote
the $f$-pull-back of $\mathcal{S}$ to $M_1$ by $\mathcal{S}^f$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Notations and conventions

nodes.name: Pull-back of a section
nodes.statement:
Given a section $s\in
\Gamma(M_2,\mathcal{S})$, we denote its $f$-pullback by $s^f\in
\Gamma(M_1,\mathcal{S}^f)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Notations and conventions

nodes.name: Pull-back of a morphism
nodes.statement:
Given $T\in {\rm Hom}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}')$, where $\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}'$ are
vector bundles defined on $M_2$, we denote the $f$-pullback of $T$ by
$T^f\in {\rm Hom}(\mathcal{S}^f,(\mathcal{S}')^f)$.

Let $\mathrm{Met}_{p,q}(W)$ denote the set of

bundle $W$ of rank ${\rm rk} W=p+q$.

Let $\mathrm{Met}(W)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \sqcup_{p,q\geq 0,

metrics on $W$.

Given a

nodes.name: Kaluza-Klein spaces as auxiliary data
nodes.statement:
Throughout the paper, we use the mathematical concept of
``Kaluza-Klein space'', which is well-established in the mathematics
and mathematical physics literature (see, for example,
\cite{Bourguignon,Hogan,Betounes1,Betounes2,Besse}). Such spaces were
initially defined and studied in the context of mathematical
foundations of Kaluza-Klein theories, which arise by reducing a
higher-dimensional theory of gravity on such a manifold. In the present
paper, such spaces are used merely as convenient auxiliary
mathematical data which parameterize a GESM theory, despite the
historical context in which they were introduced initially. Throughout
the paper, no reduction of any putative higher dimensional theory on
such spaces is ever suggested or performed.
nodes.section: 1.1 Notations and conventions

nodes.name: Space-time (M,g)
nodes.statement: Let $(M,g)$ be a connected four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Total space E
nodes.statement:
Let
$E$ be a connected manifold of dimension $\dim E=n+4$, where $n>0$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Surjective submersion
nodes.statement:
Recall that a smooth map $\pi:E\rightarrow M$ is called a {\em
  surjective submersion} if $\pi$ is surjective and the linear map
$\mathrm{d}_e \pi\colon T_e E\rightarrow T_{\pi(e)} M$ is surjective for all
$e\in E$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics
differentia:
the linear map $\mathrm{d}_e \pi\colon T_e E\rightarrow T_{\pi(e)} M$ is surjective for all
$e\in E$

nodes.name: Connected fibers
nodes.statement:
We shall always assume that the fibers of $\pi$ are
connected.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Vertical distribution
nodes.statement:
Let $\pi:E\rightarrow M$ be a surjective submersion with connected fibers.  The
{\em vertical distribution} of $\pi$ is the rank $n$ distribution
$V\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \ker (\mathrm{d} \pi)\subset T E$ defined on $E$, which is Frobenius
integrable and integrates to the foliation whose leaves are the fibers
of $\pi$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics
also_stated_at:
For any surjective submersion $\pi:E\rightarrow M$ with $\dim E>\dim
M$ and connected fibers, let $V \stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \ker (\mathrm{d} \pi)\subset TE $
denote the vertical distribution of $\pi$.

nodes.name: pi-positive metric
nodes.statement:
A Lorentzian metric $h$ on $E$ is called {\em
  $\pi$-positive} if its restriction to each fiber of $\pi$ is
positive-definite.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics
differentia:
its restriction to each fiber of $\pi$ is
positive-definite

nodes.name: Horizontal distribution H(h)
nodes.statement:
In this case, the $h$-orthogonal complement
$H:=H(h)$ of $V$ inside $TE$ is a distribution of rank four called the
{\em horizontal distribution} of $\pi$ determined by $h$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Vertical and horizontal metrics
nodes.statement:
Let $h_V$
and $h_H$ denote the metrics induced by $h$ on $V$ and $H$, which we
call the {\em vertical} and {\em horizontal} metrics induced by
$h$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Isomorphism (dpi)_H
nodes.statement:
Hence the restriction
$\mathrm{d}\pi|_H$ of $\mathrm{d} \pi$ to $H$ induces a based isomorphism of vector
bundles $(\mathrm{d}\pi)_H\colon H\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow} (TM)^\pi$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Lorentzian submersion
nodes.statement:
Let $h$ be a $\pi$-positive Lorentzian metric on $E$. 
The surjective submersion $\pi:E\rightarrow M$ is called a {\em
  Lorentzian submersion} from $(E,h)$ to $(M,g)$ if the bundle
isomorphism $(\mathrm{d}\pi)_H$ is an isometry from $(H,h_H)$ to
$((TM)^\pi,g^\pi)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Kaluza-Klein metric
nodes.statement:
A {\em Kaluza-Klein metric} for the surjective submersion
$\pi:E\rightarrow M$ relative to the Lorentzian metric $g\in
\mathrm{Met}_{3,1}(M)$ is a $\pi$-positive Lorentzian metric $h$ on $E$
which makes $\pi$ into a Lorentzian submersion from $(E,h)$ to
$(M,g)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics
differentia:
makes $\pi$ into a Lorentzian submersion from $(E,h)$ to
$(M,g)$

nodes.name: Horizontal lift
nodes.statement:
Any horizontal distribution $H$ defines a horizontal lift of vector
fields, which takes $Q\in \mathcal{X}(M)$ into the unique horizontal vector
field $\bar{Q}\in \Gamma(E,H)$ satisfying $\mathrm{d}\pi(\bar{Q}) = Q$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Horizontal/vertical parts
nodes.statement:
Moreover, 
any vector field $X\in \mathcal{X}(E)$ decomposes uniquely as $X=X_H\oplus X_V$, 
where $X_H\in \Gamma(E,H)$ and $X_V\in \Gamma(E,V)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Restricted curvature F_H and O'Neill tensor
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Vanishing of O'Neill's tensor
nodes.statement:
A basic property of O'Neill's tensor is that it vanishes if and only
if $\mathcal{F}_H$ does.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics
conclusions:
it vanishes if and only
if $\mathcal{F}_H$ does

nodes.name: Complete horizontal distribution
nodes.statement:
The distribution $H$ is called {\em complete} if the flow $T$ defined
by horizontal lifts of vector fields is globally-defined, which
amounts to the condition that {\em any} curve in $M$ lifts to a
horizontal curve in $E$ through any point lying in the fiber above its
source.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics
differentia:
the flow $T$ defined
by horizontal lifts of vector fields is globally-defined

nodes.name: Ehresmann's theorem
nodes.statement:
When $H$ is complete, it follows from a result of
\cite{Ehresmann} that $\pi$ is a fiber bundle, though its structure
group need not be a finite-dimensional Lie group.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics
conclusions: $\pi$ is a fiber bundle

nodes.name: Ehresmann connection and transport
nodes.statement:
In this case, $H$ is
an Ehresmann connection for $\pi$ and $T$ is called its Ehresmann
transport.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics

nodes.name: Reckziegel's fiber bundle theorem
nodes.statement:
Reference \cite{Reckziegel} shows that a sufficient
condition for $H$ to be complete and for the structure group to be a
finite-dimensional Lie group is that the fibers of $\pi$ be
geodesically complete and totally geodesic connected submanifolds of
$(E,h)$. In this case the Ehresmann transport $T$ is isometric, which
means that $T_\gamma$ is an isometry from $E_{\gamma(0)}$ to
$E_{\gamma(1)}$ for any path $\gamma\in \mathcal{P}(M)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Lorentzian submersions and Kaluza-Klein metrics
assumptions:
the fibers of $\pi$ be
geodesically complete and totally geodesic connected submanifolds of
$(E,h)$
conclusions:
$H$ to be complete and for the structure group to be a
finite-dimensional Lie group
the Ehresmann transport $T$ is isometric

nodes.name: Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein space
nodes.statement:
A {\em Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein space} over $(M,g)$ is a Lorentzian
submersion $\pi:(E,h)\rightarrow (M,g)$ such that $(E,h)$ is connected
and such that the fibers of $\pi$ are geodesically complete and
totally geodesic connected submanifolds of $(E,h)$. The Kaluza-Klein
space is called {\em integrable} if the horizontal distribution
$H(h)\subset TE$ defined by $h$ is Frobenius integrable.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
differentia:
the fibers of $\pi$ are geodesically complete and
totally geodesic connected submanifolds of $(E,h)$
also_stated_at:
By definition, a {\em Kaluza-Klein space} over a Lorentzian
manifold $(M,g)$ is a surjective submersion $\pi:E\rightarrow M$ whose total
space $E$ is endowed with a Lorentzian metric $h$ (known as a {\em
  Kaluza-Klein metric}) such that $\pi$ is a pseudo-Riemannian
submersion \cite{ONeillBook} from $(E,h)$ to $(M,g)$, whose fibers are
totally geodesic Riemannian connected submanifolds of $(E,h)$.

nodes.name: Model fiber (M,G)
nodes.statement:
Let $m_0$ be fixed point of $M$ and let $\mathcal{M}\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=}
E_{m_0}=\pi^{-1}(\{m_0\})$ and $\mathcal{G}\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} h|_{E_{m_0}}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces

nodes.name: Proof that h is determined by g, G, H
nodes.statement:
As mentioned
above, the results of \cite{Reckziegel} imply that $H$ is a complete
Ehresmann connection, that $\pi$ is a fiber bundle and that the
transport $T$ is isometric. Hence the restriction $h_m\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} h|_{E_m}$
of $h$ to the fibers of $E$ is uniquely determined by $\mathcal{G}$ and by
$T$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
nodes.statement_short: Reckziegel's result gives isometric transport, so fiber metrics are transported from G.

nodes.name: Kaluza-Klein metric determined by g, G and H
nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Proof of the classification of Kaluza-Klein spaces
nodes.statement:
Then $\Pi$ is a principal $G$-bundle (known as the
{\em holonomy bundle} of $H$ relative to $m_0$) under the obvious
right action of $G$. Moreover, the Ehresmann connection $H$ induces a
principal connection $\theta$ on $\Pi$. Conversely, let $\rho$ be the
isometric action of $G$ on $\mathcal{M}$ given by the inclusion $G\subseteq
\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$. Then the associated bundle construction associates to
a principal bundle $\Pi$ with principal connection $\theta$ the fiber
bundle $E_\Pi\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \Pi\times_\rho \mathcal{M}$ with induced Ehresmann
connection $H_\theta$. The two correspondences described above give
mutually quasi-inverse functors between the groupoid of Kaluza-Klein
spaces over $(M,g)$ which have typical fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ and are
endowed with a horizontal distribution $H$ with holonomy $G\subseteq
\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ and the groupoid of principal $G$-bundles $\Pi$ defined
over $M$ and endowed with a principal connection $\theta$ together
with an embedding $G\subseteq \mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ up to conjugation. Hence:
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
nodes.statement_short: Construct mutually quasi-inverse functors: holonomy bundle with induced connection, and associated bundle construction.

nodes.name: Holonomy bundle with connection
nodes.statement:
Then $\Pi$ is a principal $G$-bundle (known as the
{\em holonomy bundle} of $H$ relative to $m_0$) under the obvious
right action of $G$. Moreover, the Ehresmann connection $H$ induces a
principal connection $\theta$ on $\Pi$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
nodes.statement_short: The holonomy bundle is a principal G-bundle with connection induced by H.

nodes.name: Associated bundle construction
nodes.statement:
Conversely, let $\rho$ be the
isometric action of $G$ on $\mathcal{M}$ given by the inclusion $G\subseteq
\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$. Then the associated bundle construction associates to
a principal bundle $\Pi$ with principal connection $\theta$ the fiber
bundle $E_\Pi\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \Pi\times_\rho \mathcal{M}$ with induced Ehresmann
connection $H_\theta$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
nodes.statement_short: Conversely, the associated bundle of (Pi, theta) gives a fiber bundle with Ehresmann connection.

nodes.name: Equivalence of groupoids
nodes.statement:
The two correspondences described above give
mutually quasi-inverse functors between the groupoid of Kaluza-Klein
spaces over $(M,g)$ which have typical fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ and are
endowed with a horizontal distribution $H$ with holonomy $G\subseteq
\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ and the groupoid of principal $G$-bundles $\Pi$ defined
over $M$ and endowed with a principal connection $\theta$ together
with an embedding $G\subseteq \mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ up to conjugation. Hence:
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
nodes.statement_short: The two constructions are quasi-inverse functors between the groupoids.

nodes.name: Classification of Kaluza-Klein spaces by principal bundles
nodes.statement:
Let $g$ be a fixed Lorentzian metric on $M$. Then isomorphism classes
of Kaluza-Klein spaces over $(M,g)$ with typical fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ and
horizontal distribution $H$ having Ehresmann holonomy contained in
$\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ are in bijection with isomorphism classes of principal
$G$-bundles $\Pi$ defined over $M$ and endowed with a principal
connection $\theta$ whose holonomy is embedded in $\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$. 
Moreover, $H$ is integrable if and only if $\theta$ is
flat.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
assumptions: Let $g$ be a fixed Lorentzian metric on $M$.
conclusions:
isomorphism classes
of Kaluza-Klein spaces over $(M,g)$ with typical fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ and
horizontal distribution $H$ having Ehresmann holonomy contained in
$\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ are in bijection with isomorphism classes of principal
$G$-bundles $\Pi$ defined over $M$ and endowed with a principal
connection $\theta$ whose holonomy is embedded in $\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$

$H$ is integrable if and only if $\theta$ is
flat
nodes.statement_short: Kaluza-Klein spaces with given fiber correspond bijectively to principal bundles with connection; integrability iff flatness.

nodes.name: Trivial bundle E^0
nodes.statement:
Let $E^{0} \stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=}
M\times\mathcal{M}$ and let $\pi^0:M\times \mathcal{M}\rightarrow M$ and
$p^0:M\times\mathcal{M}\rightarrow \mathcal{M}$ denote the canonical
projections.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces

nodes.name: Vertical distribution V^0
nodes.statement:
Let $V^0=(T\mathcal{M})^{p^0}$ denote the vertical
distribution of $\pi^0$, which is endowed with the pull-back metric
$\mathcal{G}^{p^0}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces

nodes.name: Topologically trivial Kaluza-Klein space
nodes.statement:
A {\em topologically trivial Kaluza-Klein space} over $(M,g)$ with
fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ is a Kaluza-Klein space of the form
$\pi^0:(E^0,h^{0})\rightarrow (M,g)$, whose vertical metric is the
pull-back metric $h_{V^0}\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \mathcal{G}^{p^0}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
differentia:
vertical metric is the
pull-back metric $h_{V^0}\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \mathcal{G}^{p^0}$

nodes.name: Fiber transport hat T
nodes.statement:
For any $\gamma\in \mathcal{P}(M)$
and all $p\in \mathcal{M}$, we define:
\begin{equation} T_\gamma(\gamma(0),p)=(\gamma(1),{\hat T}_\gamma(p))~~, 
\end{equation}
where ${\hat T}_\gamma\in \mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ satisfy ${\hat T}_{\gamma_1\gamma_2}={\hat T}_{\gamma_1}\circ {\hat T}_{\gamma_2}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces

nodes.name: Transport in trivial bundle
nodes.statement: T_\gamma(\gamma(0),p)=(\gamma(1),{\hat T}_\gamma(p))~~,
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
nodes.label: hatT

nodes.name: Product Kaluza-Klein space
nodes.statement:
The {\em product Kaluza-Klein space} over $(M,g)$ with fiber
$(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ is the topologically trivial Kaluza-Klein space
$\pi^0:(E^0,h^0_{\mathrm{triv}})\rightarrow (M,g)$ with fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$
whose horizontal distribution is the trivial integrable Ehresmann
connection $H^0_{\mathrm{triv}} \stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} (T M)^{\pi^0}$, with induced horizontal
metric $h^0_{\mathrm{triv}}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
differentia:
horizontal distribution is the trivial integrable Ehresmann
connection $H^0_{\mathrm{triv}} \stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} (T M)^{\pi^0}$

nodes.name: Proof that the product KK metric is the product metric
nodes.statement:
For any $p\in \mathcal{M}$, the horizontal lift through $(\gamma(0),p)\in
E^0_{\gamma(0)}$ of any path $\gamma\in \mathcal{P}(M)$ defined by the
trivial Ehresmann connection $H^0$ is the path given by
$\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{p, \mathrm{triv}}(s)=(\gamma(s),p)$ for all $s\in [0,1]$. Hence the
Ehresmann transport $T^0_\gamma$ defined by $H^0$ is given by ${\hat
T}^0_{\gamma}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{M}}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
nodes.statement_short: Horizontal lifts of the trivial connection are constant in the fiber, so transport is the identity.

nodes.name: Product Kaluza-Klein metric equals g x G
nodes.statement:
This implies that the Kaluza-Klein metric
$h^0_{\mathrm{triv}}=h_{g, \mathcal{G}, H^0_{\mathrm{triv}}}$ equals the product metric
$g\times \mathcal{G}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
conclusions:
the Kaluza-Klein metric
$h^0_{\mathrm{triv}}=h_{g, \mathcal{G}, H^0_{\mathrm{triv}}}$ equals the product metric
$g\times \mathcal{G}$

nodes.name: Proof of the character variety classification
nodes.statement:
As explained above, integrable Kaluza-Klein spaces correspond to flat
principal $G$-bundles $(\Pi,\theta)$ defined over $M$ together with an
embedding $G\subseteq \mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
nodes.statement_short: Combine the principal-bundle classification with the holonomy classification of flat bundles.

nodes.name: Classification of flat principal bundles by holonomy
nodes.statement:
It is well-known that flat
principal $G$-bundles are classified up to isomorphism by their
holonomy morphism $\mathrm{Hol}_{P,\theta}:\pi_1(M)\rightarrow G$, considered
up to the conjugation action of $G$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
conclusions:
flat
principal $G$-bundles are classified up to isomorphism by their
holonomy morphism $\mathrm{Hol}_{P,\theta}:\pi_1(M)\rightarrow G$, considered
up to the conjugation action of $G$

nodes.name: Integrable KK spaces classified by character variety
nodes.statement:
Hence the set of isomorphism
classes of integrable Kaluza-Klein spaces over $(M,g)$ with
fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ and Ehresmann holonomy contained in 
$\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ is in bijection with the character variety:
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})}(M)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} {\rm Hom}(\pi_1(M),\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G}))/\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})\, .
\end{equation*}
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
conclusions:
the set of isomorphism
classes of integrable Kaluza-Klein spaces over $(M,g)$ with
fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ and Ehresmann holonomy contained in 
$\mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ is in bijection with the character variety
nodes.statement_short: Integrable Kaluza-Klein spaces with fiber (M,G) are classified by the character variety Hom(pi_1(M), Iso(M,G))/Iso(M,G).

nodes.name: Simply-connected space-time gives product spaces
nodes.statement:
When the space-time $M$ is simply-connected, any integrable
Kaluza-Klein space over $(M,g)$ is isomorphic with a product space
(see below). In that case, we necessarily have $G=1$ (the trivial
group) and $H$ is gauge-equivalent with the trivial Ehresmann
connection.
nodes.section: 2.2 Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein spaces
conclusions:
any integrable
Kaluza-Klein space over $(M,g)$ is isomorphic with a product space

we necessarily have $G=1$ (the trivial
group) and $H$ is gauge-equivalent with the trivial Ehresmann
connection

nodes.name: Vertical scalar potential
nodes.statement:
A \emph{vertical scalar potential} for $\pi$ is a smooth $T$-invariant
real-valued function $\mathbf{\Phi} \in \mathcal{C}^\infty(E,\mathbb{R})$ defined on the total
space $E$ of $\pi$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Vertical scalar potentials and scalar bundles
also_stated_at:
A {\em vertical scalar potential} on
$\pi$ is a smooth real-valued map $\mathbf{\Phi}$ defined on the total space
$E$ of $\pi$ such that the restrictions of $\mathbf{\Phi}$ to the fibers of
$\pi$ are related by the Ehresmann transport and hence can be
identified with a smooth real-valued function $\Phi$ defined on $\mathcal{M}$, 
which is invariant under the holonomy group $G$.

nodes.label: Vvert

nodes.statement:
In
particular, the isomorphism type of the scalar structure\footnote{As

nodes.name: Proof that grad Phi is vertical
nodes.statement:
Relation \eqref{Vvert} amounts to $\mathrm{d} \mathbf{\Phi} (X)=0$ for all
$X\in\Gamma(X,H)$, i.e. $\mathrm{d} \mathbf{\Phi} \circ P_H=0$. Since
$P_V+P_H=\mathrm{id}_{TE}$, this gives $\mathrm{d} \mathbf{\Phi}=\mathrm{d} \mathbf{\Phi} \circ P_V$, which
shows that $\mathrm{d} \mathbf{\Phi}$ can be viewed as an element of
$\Gamma(E,V^\ast)$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Vertical scalar potentials and scalar bundles
nodes.statement_short: Horizontal annihilation means dPhi factors through the vertical projector.

nodes.name: Gradient of the vertical potential is vertical
nodes.section: 2.3 Vertical scalar potentials and scalar bundles
conclusions: the gradient of $\mathbf{\Phi}$ is a vertical vector field

nodes.name: Scalar bundle
nodes.statement:
A {\em scalar bundle} over $(M,g)$ is a pair $(\pi:(E,h)\rightarrow
(M,g),\mathbf{\Phi})$, where $\pi$ is a Kaluza-Klein space and $\mathbf{\Phi}$ is a
vertical scalar potential for $\pi$. The scalar bundle is called {\em
integrable} if the Kaluza-Klein space $\pi$ is integrable.
nodes.section: 2.3 Vertical scalar potentials and scalar bundles
differentia:
$\mathbf{\Phi}$ is a
vertical scalar potential for $\pi$

nodes.name: Type of a scalar bundle
nodes.statement:
The isomorphism type of the scalar structures $(E_m,h_m,\Phi_m)$
(which, as explained above, does not depend on the point $m\in M$) is
called the {\em type} of the scalar bundle and will be generally
denoted by $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G},\Phi)$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Vertical scalar potentials and scalar bundles

nodes.name: Proof of the classification of integrable scalar bundles
nodes.statement:
The classification of integrable
Kaluza-Klein spaces immediately implies the following.
nodes.section: 2.3 Vertical scalar potentials and scalar bundles
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the classification of integrable Kaluza-Klein spaces.

nodes.name: Classification of integrable scalar bundles
nodes.section: 2.3 Vertical scalar potentials and scalar bundles
conclusions:
Integrable scalar bundles defined over $(M,g)$ and having type
$(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G},\Phi)$ are classified up to isomorphism by the points of the
character variety
nodes.statement_short: Integrable scalar bundles of a given type are classified by the character variety for Iso(M,G,Phi).

nodes.name: Geodesically convex set
nodes.statement:
Recall that an open subset $U$ of a pseudo-Riemannian
manifold is called {\em geodesically convex} \cite{ONeillBook} if it
is a normal neighborhood for each of its points.
nodes.section: 2.4 Special trivializing atlases for a Kaluza-Klein space and for a scalar bundle

nodes.name: Unique geodesics in convex sets
nodes.statement:
If $U$ is convex,
then for any two points $p,q\in U$ there exists a unique geodesic
segment which is contained in $U$ and which connects $p$ and $q$.
nodes.section: 2.4 Special trivializing atlases for a Kaluza-Klein space and for a scalar bundle
conclusions:
for any two points $p,q\in U$ there exists a unique geodesic
segment which is contained in $U$ and which connects $p$ and $q$

nodes.name: Convex cover
nodes.statement:
A {\em convex
  cover} of a pseudo-Riemannian manifold is an cover by open and
geodesically convex sets which has the property that any nontrivial
intersection of two of its elements is geodesically convex.
nodes.section: 2.4 Special trivializing atlases for a Kaluza-Klein space and for a scalar bundle

nodes.name: Existence of refining convex covers (O'Neill Lemma 5.10)
nodes.statement:
Given
any open cover $\mathfrak{V}$ of a pseudo-Riemannian manifold, there
exists a convex cover $\mathfrak{U}$ such that any element of
$\mathfrak{U}$ is contained in some element of $\mathfrak{V}$
\cite[Lemma 5.10]{ONeillBook}.
nodes.section: 2.4 Special trivializing atlases for a Kaluza-Klein space and for a scalar bundle
assumptions: any open cover $\mathfrak{V}$ of a pseudo-Riemannian manifold
conclusions:
there
exists a convex cover $\mathfrak{U}$ such that any element of
$\mathfrak{U}$ is contained in some element of $\mathfrak{V}$

Let $\mathfrak{U}=\left( U_\alpha\right)_{\alpha \in I}$ be

Fix points $m_{\alpha}\in U_\alpha$ and paths
$\lambda^{\alpha}\in \mathcal{P}(M)$ such that
$\lambda^{\alpha}(0)=m_{\alpha}$ and $\lambda^{\alpha}(1)=m_0$.

nodes.name: Radial geodesics gamma_m^alpha
nodes.statement:
For
any $m\in U_\alpha$, let $\gamma_m^{\alpha}:[0,1]\rightarrow U_\alpha$
be the unique smooth geodesic contained in $U_\alpha$ such that
$\gamma_m^{\alpha}(0)=m$ and $\gamma_m^{\alpha}(1)=m_\alpha$.

$E^0_{\alpha}\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} U_\alpha\times \mathcal{M}$ and $\pi^0_{\alpha}\colon
E_{\alpha}^{0}\rightarrow U_\alpha$, $p^0_{\alpha}\colon
E^0_{\alpha}\rightarrow \mathcal{M}$ be the projections on the first and
second factors.

nodes.name: Special trivializing maps q_alpha
nodes.statement:
Define diffeomorphisms
$q_\alpha:E_{\alpha}\rightarrow U_\alpha\times \mathcal{M}$ through:
\begin{equation} q_\alpha(e)=(\pi(e), {\hat q}_\alpha(e))\, , \quad  \forall\, e\in E_\alpha\, ,
\end{equation}
where ${\hat q}_\alpha\colon E_\alpha\rightarrow \mathcal{M}$ is given by the
following differentiable surjective map:
\begin{equation} \hat{q}_\alpha(e)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} p^0_{\alpha}\circ (T_{\lambda^{\alpha}}\circ T_{\gamma^{\alpha}_{\pi(e)}})(e)=p^0_{\alpha}\circ T_{\lambda^{\alpha}\circ \gamma^{\alpha}_{\pi(e)}}(e)\in  \mathcal{M}\, , \qquad \forall\, e\in E_\alpha\, .
\end{equation}

nodes.statement: q_\alpha(e)=(\pi(e), {\hat q}_\alpha(e))\, , \quad  \forall\, e\in E_\alpha\, ,

nodes.name: Fiber isometry hat q_alpha(m)
nodes.statement:
The restriction ${\hat q}_{\alpha}(m)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} {\hat

is an isometry from $(E_m,h_m)$ to $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ which is given

{\hat q}_{\alpha}(m)(e_{m})=p^{0}_{\alpha}\circ T_{\lambda^{\alpha}\circ \gamma^{\alpha}_{m}}(m\times e_{m})\, , \quad \forall\, e_{m}\in E_m\, . 
\end{equation*}

nodes.name: Proof of the integrable special atlas proposition
nodes.statement:
When the Kaluza-Klein space $\pi$ is integrable, the Ehresmann
transport depends only on the homotopy class of curves in $M$.  In
this case, $T_{c^{\alpha\beta}_m}$ is independent of the point $m\in
U_\alpha\cap U_\beta$ since $U_\alpha\cap U_\beta$ is path connected
and hence the homotopy class of $c^{\alpha\beta}_m$ does not depend on
$m$. Moreover, integrability of $H$ implies that $H_{\alpha}^{0}$
coincide with the trivial Ehresmann connections $H_{\alpha}^{\mathrm{triv}}$
of $\pi^0_{\alpha}$.  In this case, $\pi^0_{\alpha}\colon
(E^0_{\alpha}, h_\alpha)\rightarrow (U_\alpha,g_\alpha)$ is a product
Kaluza-Klein space and $q_\alpha$ is an isometry from $(E_{\alpha},
h_\alpha)$ to $(U_\alpha\times\mathcal{M},g_\alpha\times \mathcal{G})$. Thus:

nodes.name: Special atlases of integrable Kaluza-Klein spaces
nodes.statement:
Let $\pi:(E,h)\rightarrow (M,g)$ be an integrable Kaluza-Klein

trivializing atlas consist on isometries from $(E_{\alpha}, h_\alpha)$

functions $\mathbf{g}_{\alpha\beta}$ defined by such an atlas are constant on
$U_\alpha\cap U_\beta$. In particular, $\pi$ is locally isomorphic
with a product Kaluza-Klein space.

nodes.name: Section sigma model
nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Ordinary Lagrange density and tension field
nodes.statement:
The ordinary Lagrange density and tension field of $s\in\Gamma(\pi)$
are defined similarly to their vertical counterparts except that there
is no vertical projection involved. More precisely, we define:
\begin{equation*}
e_{\mathbf{\Phi}}(g,h,s)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}_{g} s^\ast (h)+\mathbf{\Phi}^s\, ,
\end{equation*}
as well as:
\begin{equation*}
\tau(g, h, s)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \mathrm{Tr}_{g}\nabla \mathrm{d} s \in \Gamma(M,TE^s)\, ,
\end{equation*}
where $\nabla$ denotes the connection on $T^{\ast}M\otimes TE^{s}$
induced by the Levi-Civita connection on $(M,g)$ and the $s$-pullback
of the Levi-Civita connection on $(E,h)$. For simplicity we will
sometimes drop the explicit dependence on $g$ and $h$ in
$e_{\mathbf{\Phi}}(g,h,s)$, $\tau(g, h, s)$ etc.

nodes.name: Modified scalar sigma model
nodes.statement:
The {\em modified scalar sigma model} determined by $(M,g)$,
$(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ and $H^0$ is defined by the action:
\begin{equation*}
S^{H^0}_{\mathrm{sc},\mathbf{\Phi}, U^0}[\varphi]=S_{\mathrm{sc},\pi^0, \mathbf{\Phi}, U^0}[\mathrm{graph}(\varphi)]\, .
\end{equation*}
for any relatively compact open set $U^0\subset M$, where
$S_{\mathrm{sc}, \pi, \mathbf{\Phi}, U^0}$ is the action of the section sigma model of
the topologically trivial Kaluza-Klein space $\pi^0\colon
(E^0,h^0)\rightarrow (M,g)$ with fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ and horizontal
distribution $H^0$.

nodes.name: H^0-pseudoharmonic map
nodes.statement:
Let $H^0$ be any horizontal distribution for the trivial bundle

(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ is called {\em $H^0$-pseudoharmonic} if the graph $s^0$ of
$\varphi$ is a pseudo-harmonic section of the topologically trivial
Kaluza-Klein space $\pi^0\colon (E^0,h^{0})\rightarrow (M,g)$ with
fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$, where $h^{0}$ is the metric on $E^{0}$ determined
by $H^{0}, \mathcal{G}$ and $g$.

nodes.name: Modified sigma model solutions are H^0-pseudoharmonic

nodes.name: Product case reduces to ordinary sigma model
nodes.statement:
Let $\pi^0:(E^0\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} M\times\mathcal{M}, h^0\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} g\times \mathcal{G})\rightarrow
(M,g)$ be the product Kaluza-Klein space with fiber $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$
defined over $(M,g)$ and horizontal distribution $H^{0}_{\mathrm{triv}}$. For
any $s\in \Gamma(\pi^0)$, we have $s^\ast(h)=\varphi^\ast (\mathcal{G})$ and
$\mathrm{d}^v s=\mathrm{d} \varphi$, where $\varphi=\mathrm{ungraph}(s)=p^0\circ s$. Thus
$e^v(s)=e(\varphi)$ and $\tau^v(s)=\tau(\varphi)$. Moreover, we have
$\mathbf{\Phi}=\Phi\circ p^0$ for some $\Phi\in \mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathcal{M},\mathbb{R})$. Hence the
section sigma model action \eqref{Ssc} reduces to the action of an
ordinary sigma model of maps from $(M,g)$ to $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$, while the
equations of motion \eqref{sceom} reduce to those of an ordinary sigma
model. Setting $\Phi=0$, we conclude that a map
$\varphi:(M,g)\rightarrow (\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ is $H^0_{\mathrm{triv}}$-pseudoharmonic if
and only if it is pseudo-harmonic.
nodes.section: 3.3 A modified sigma model for maps
nodes.statement_short: For the product Kaluza-Klein space the section sigma model is the ordinary sigma model; H^0_triv-pseudoharmonic equals pseudo-harmonic.

\end{equation}

nodes.name: Local equivalence of equations of motion (integrable case)
nodes.statement:

$\pi$ induce isomorphisms of sheaves:

\mathrm{Conf}_\pi\simeq \mathbf{Conf}_{\mathcal{M}}\, , \quad \mathrm{Sol}_{\pi,\mathbf{\Phi}}\simeq \mathbf{Sol}_{\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G},\Phi}^{g}\, .

which present $\mathbf{Conf}_{\mathcal{M}}$ and $\mathbf{Sol}_{\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G},\Phi}$ respectively as
the sheaves of configurations and solutions of the section sigma model

nodes.name: Classical scalar locally-geometric U-fold
nodes.statement:
A {\em classical scalar locally-geometric U-fold} of type
$(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G},\Phi)$ is a smooth global solution $s\in \Gamma(\pi)$ of the
equations of motion \eqref{sceom} of the section sigma model defined
by an {\em integrable} bundle of scalar data ($\pi:(E,h)\rightarrow
(M,g),\mathbf{\Phi})$ having type $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G},\Phi)$.

The {\em extended horizontal transport} along a path
$\gamma\in \mathcal{P}(M)$ is the unbased isomorphism of vector bundles

nodes.name: Duality bundle
nodes.statement:
Let $\pi\colon (E,h)\to (M,g)$ be a Kaluza-Klein space. A
\emph{duality bundle} $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ is a flat symplectic vector bundle
$\boldsymbol{\Delta} = (\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}},\boldsymbol{\omega},\mathbf{D})$ over $E$. Let $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{1}$ and

nodes.name: Proof of the isomorphism type of Theta and Psi
nodes.statement:
Let us fix $m_{0}\in M$. The fact that the restriction $\Psi_{m_{0}}$
of the fundamental bundle field $\mathbf{\Psi}$ to $E_{m_{0}}$ is a vector
field over $E_{m_{0}}$ taking values on $End(\mathcal{S}_{m_{0}})$ together
with the fact that the extended horizontal transport $\mathbf{T}_{\gamma}$
preserves the flat symplectic connection on $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}$ and covers
isometries, implies:
\begin{equation} \mathbf{T}_{\gamma} \cdot \Theta_{m_{0}} = \Theta_{m}\, , \qquad \forall\, m\in M\, ,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation} \mathbf{T}_{\gamma} \cdot\Psi_{m_{0}} = \Psi_{m}\, , \qquad \forall\, m\in M\, ,
\end{equation}
where $\gamma\in\mathcal{P}(M)$ is a path in $M$ with initial point $\gamma(0)
= m_{0}$ and final point $\gamma(1) = m$. We conclude that the
isomorphism type of the restriction of the fundamental bundle form
$\mathbf{\Theta}$ and the fundamental bundle field $\mathbf{\Psi}$ to $E_{m}$ does not
depend on the point and hence will be denoted by $\Theta$ and $\Psi$,
respectively.

\begin{remark} Equation \eqref{eq:isoTheta} follows from the following
computation\footnote{Equation \eqref{eq:isoPsi} can be proved
  similarly.}:
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{T}_{\gamma} \cdot \Theta_{m_{0}} = \mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\cdot D^{\mathrm{ad}}_{m_{0}}(\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\cdot\mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\cdot J_{m_{0}}) = \mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\cdot D^{\mathrm{ad}}_{m_{0}}(\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\cdot J_{m}) = D^{\mathrm{ad}}_{m} J_{m} = \Theta_{m}\, ,
\end{equation*}
where we have used the fact that $\mathbf{T}_{\gamma}$ preserves $D_{m_{0}}$ and $D_{m}$, i.e.:
\begin{equation} D^{\mathrm{ad}}_{m}(\xi)  =  \mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\cdot D^{\mathrm{ad}}_{m_{0}} (\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\cdot\xi) = \mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\cdot D^{\mathrm{ad}}_{m_{0}} (\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\circ\xi \circ T_{\gamma})\, , \quad\forall\,\, \xi\in\Gamma(E_{m},\mathcal{S}_{m})\, ,
\end{equation}
as well as the relations:
\begin{eqnarray} & (\mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\cdot J_{m_{0}})(\xi) = \mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\cdot J_{m_{0}}(\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\cdot\xi) = \mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\cdot (J_{m_{0}} \circ\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\circ \xi \circ T_{\gamma}) \nonumber\\
& = \mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\circ (J_{m_{0}} \circ\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\circ \xi \circ T_{\gamma})\circ T^{-1}_{\gamma} = \mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\circ J_{m_{0}} \circ\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\circ \xi = J_{m}(\xi)\, ,
\end{eqnarray}
which hold for all $\xi\in \Gamma(E_{m},\mathcal{S}_{m})$. Notice that the
$\mathbf{T}_{\gamma}$-action symbols $``\cdot"$ and $``\circ"$ in equations
\eqref{eq:D0m} and \eqref{eq:J0m} have a different meaning depending
on the step and the sections involved. In equation \eqref{eq:D0m} we
have:
\begin{equation*}
D^{\mathrm{ad}}_{m_{0}} (\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\circ\xi \circ T_{\gamma}) \in \Omega^{1}(E_{m_{0}},\mathcal{S}_{m_{0}})
\end{equation*}
and evaluating on a vector field $X\in\mathfrak{X}(E_{m})$ we obtain:
\begin{equation*}
\iota_{X} D^{\mathrm{ad}}_{m}(\xi) = \mathbf{T}_{\gamma}\circ \left(\iota_{T^{-1}_{\gamma\ast}X} D^{\mathrm{ad}}_{m_{0}} (\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\circ\xi \circ T_{\gamma})\right)\circ T^{-1}_{\gamma}\in \Gamma(E_{m},\mathcal{S}_{m})\, .
\end{equation*}
Likewise, in the second step of equation \eqref{eq:J0m} we use:
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\cdot\xi = \mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\circ \xi \circ T_{\gamma}\in \Gamma(E_{m_{0}},\mathcal{S}_{m_{0}}) \, , \quad \xi\in \Gamma(E_{m},\mathcal{S}_{m})\, ,
\end{equation*}
where $\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}$ in the left hand side acts through
$``\cdot"$ as the isomorphism of modules:
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\colon \Gamma(E_{m},\mathcal{S}_m) \to \Gamma(E_{m_{0}},\mathcal{S}_{m_{0}})\, ,
\end{equation*}
whereas $\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}$ in the right-hand-side acts through $``\circ"$
as composition with the unbased automorphism
$\mathbf{T}^{-1}_{\gamma}\colon \mathcal{S}_{m}\to \mathcal{S}_{m_{0}}$ of vector bundles
covering $T^{-1}_{\gamma}$. 
\end{remark}

\noindent
The following proposition follows from the previous discussion and
summarizes the isomorphism type of a fundamental bundle field
$\mathbf{\Psi}$. Similar remarks apply for the fundamental bundle form
$\mathbf{\Theta}$.

nodes.name: Generalized Section-Maxwell theory (informal)
nodes.statement:
Before defining the complete GESM theory, we consider in this subsection
a truncated version consisting of a section sigma model coupled to a
generically non-trivial duality bundle. We call such theory a
{\em Generalized Section-Maxwell theory}, or GSM theory for short.

nodes.name: Electromagnetic field strength
nodes.statement:
Let $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}=(\pi,\mathbf{\Phi}, {\boldsymbol{\Xi}})$ be a scalar-electromagnetic bundle
with associated Kaluza-Klein space $\pi\colon (E,h)\to
(M,g)$ and let $s\in \Gamma(\pi)$ be a section of $\pi$. An {\em
electromagnetic field strength} is a two-form
$\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\in \Omega^2(M,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^s)$ having the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[1.]
\itemsep 0.0em
\item $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}$ is positively-polarized with respect to $\mathbf{J}^s$, i.e. the
  following relation is satisfied:
\begin{equation*}
\ast_g \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}=-\mathbf{J}^s\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\, .
\end{equation*}
\item $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}$ satisfies the {\em electromagnetic equation} with respect
  to $s$:
\begin{equation} \mathrm{d}_{\mathbf{D}^s} \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}=0~~.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

$\Omega^{2+,s}_{g,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}},\mathbf{J}}(M)$ denotes the space of $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^s$-valued
two-forms on $M$ which are positively-polarized with respect to
$\mathbf{J}^s$.

nodes.name: Sheaf of electromagnetic field strengths
nodes.statement:
The \emph{sheaf of electromagnetic field strengths} is the sheaf
$\mathcal{E}_{g,\mathbf{D},\mathbf{J}}^s$ of vector spaces defined as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{E}_{g,\mathbf{D},\mathbf{J}}^s(U) \stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\in \Omega^{2+,s}_{g,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}},\mathbf{J}}(U)\, , \,\, | \,\, \mathrm{d}_{\mathbf{D}^s}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}=0\}\, ,
\end{equation*}
for every open set $U\subset M$. The vector space of global
electromagnetic field strengths in $M$ is then given by
$\mathcal{E}_{g,\mathbf{D},\mathbf{J}}^s(M)$.

nodes.name: Configuration sheaf of a GSM theory
nodes.statement:
Let $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}} = (\pi,\mathbf{\Phi},{\boldsymbol{\Xi}})$ be a scalar-electromagnetic bundle with
associated Kaluza-Klein space $\pi\colon (E,h)\to (M,g)$. The {\em
configuration sheaf} $\mathrm{Conf}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}$ of a GSM theory associated to
$\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}$ is the sheaf of sets defined as follows:
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{Conf}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}(U)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \left\{ (s,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}})\, , \,\, |\,\, s\in \Gamma(\pi|_{U}) \, , \, \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\in \Omega^{2+,s}_{g,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}},\mathbf{J}}(U) \right\}\, ,
\end{equation*}
for every open set $U\subset M$.
nodes.section: 5.1 The polarization condition and the electromagnetic equation

nodes.name: GSM theory
nodes.statement:
Let $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}} = (\pi,\mathbf{\Phi},{\boldsymbol{\Xi}})$ be a scalar-electromagnetic bundle with
associated Kaluza-Klein space $\pi\colon (E,h)\to (M,g)$. The
GSM theory associated to $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}$ is defined by the following set of
partial differential equations on $(M,g)$\footnote{The meaning of the
symbol $(-,-)$ will be explained in a moment, see definition \ref{def:tep}.}:
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{E}_{S}(s,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}) \stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \tau^{v}(h,s) + (\mathrm{grad}_{h} \mathbf{\Phi})^{s}- \frac{1}{2} (\ast \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}} , \mathbf{\Psi}^s\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}) = 0\, , \quad \mathcal{E}_{K}(s,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}})\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \mathrm{d}_{\mathbf{D}^s} \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}=0\, ,
\end{equation*}
with unknowns given by pairs $(s,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}})\in \mathrm{Conf}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}(M)$.
nodes.section: 5.1 The polarization condition and the electromagnetic equation

nodes.name: Solution sheaf of a GSM theory
nodes.statement:
The {\em solution sheaf} of a GSM theory associated to a
scalar-electromagnetic bundle $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}} = (\pi,\mathbf{\Phi},{\boldsymbol{\Xi}})$ is the sheaf
of sets is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{Sol}^g_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}(U)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \{(s,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}})\in \mathrm{Conf}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}(U)\, , \,\, |\,\, \mathcal{E}_{S}(s,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}) = 0\, , \quad  \mathcal{E}_{K}(s,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}) = 0\}\, ,
\end{equation*}
for every open set $U\subset M$.
nodes.section: 5.1 The polarization condition and the electromagnetic equation

nodes.name: Configuration sheaf of a GESM theory
nodes.statement:
Let $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}} = (\pi,\mathbf{\Phi},{\boldsymbol{\Xi}})$ be a scalar-electromagnetic bundle with
associated Lorentzian submersion $\pi\colon (E,h)\to (M,g)$. The {\em
  configuration sheaf} of a GESM-theory defined by $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}$ is the sheaf
of sets given by:
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{Conf}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}(U)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \left\{ (g,s,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}})\, , \,\, |\,\, g\in\mathrm{Met}_{3,1}(U)\, , \,   s\in \Gamma(\pi|_{U}) \, , \, \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}\in \Omega^{2+,s}_{g,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}},\mathbf{J}}(U) \right\}\, ,
\end{equation*}
for every open set $U\subset M$.

nodes.name: Exterior pairing
nodes.statement:
The {\em exterior pairing} $(~,~)_g$ is the pseudo-Euclidean metric
induced by $g$ on the exterior bundle $\wedge_M$.
nodes.section: 5.2 The complete GESM theory

nodes.name: Twisted exterior pairing
nodes.statement:
The {\em twisted exterior pairing} $(~,~):=(~,~)_{g,\boldsymbol{Q}^{s}}$ is the
unique pseudo-Euclidean scalar product on the twisted exterior bundle
$\wedge_M(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{s})$ which satisfies:
\begin{equation*}
(\rho_1\otimes \xi_1,\rho_2\otimes \xi_2)_{g,\boldsymbol{Q}^{s}}=(\rho_1,\rho_2)_g \boldsymbol{Q}^{s}(\xi_1,\xi_2)\, ,
\end{equation*}
for any $\rho_1,\rho_2\in \Omega^{\bullet}(M)$ and any
$\xi_1,\xi_2\in \Gamma(M,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{s})$. Here $\boldsymbol{Q}^{s}(\xi_1,\xi_2)
= \boldsymbol{\omega}^{s}(\mathbf{J}^{s} \xi_1,\xi_2)$ and the superscript denotes pull-back by
$s$.
nodes.section: 5.2 The complete GESM theory
nodes.label: def:tep

nodes.name: W-valued twisted exterior pairing
nodes.statement:
For any vector bundle $W$, we trivially extend the twisted
exterior pairing to a $W$-valued pairing (which for simplicity we
denote by the same symbol) between the bundles $W\otimes
(\wedge_M(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{s}))$ and $\wedge_M(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{s})$. Thus:
\begin{equation*}
(e \otimes \eta_1,\eta_2)_{g,\boldsymbol{Q}^{s}} \stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=}  e \otimes (\eta_1,\eta_2)_{g,\boldsymbol{Q}^{s}}\, , \quad\forall\, e\in \Gamma(M,W)\, , \quad \forall\, \eta_1,\eta_2\in \wedge_M(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{s})\, .
\end{equation*}

nodes.name: Inner g-contraction of 2-forms

nodes.name: Twisted inner contraction
nodes.statement:
The {\em twisted inner contraction} of $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{s}$-valued 2-forms is
the unique morphism of vector bundles
$\bm{\oslash}\colon\wedge_M^2(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{s})\times_M\wedge_M^2(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{s})\rightarrow\otimes^2(T^\ast
M)$ which satisfies the condition:
\begin{equation*}
(\rho_1\otimes \xi_1)\bm{\oslash} (\rho_2\otimes \xi_2)= \boldsymbol{Q}^{s} (\xi_1,\xi_2) \rho_1 \oslash_g\rho_2\, ,
\end{equation*}
for all $\rho_1,\rho_2\in \Omega^2(M)$ and all $\xi_2,\xi_2\in \Gamma(M,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{s})$.

nodes.name: Proof of the local equivalence theorem
nodes.statement:
Given $(g_\alpha,s_\alpha,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}_\alpha)\in \mathbf{Conf}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}(U_\alpha)$, we set:
\begin{equation*}
\mathfrak{C}_{\alpha}(g_{\alpha},s_{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}_{\alpha})\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} (g_{\alpha},\varphi^\alpha,\mathcal{V}^\alpha)~~,
\end{equation*}
where $\varphi^\alpha$ and $\mathcal{V}_\alpha$ are defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item As explained in Subsection \ref{spectrivgauge}, the special
  trivializing atlas $(U_\alpha,\mathbf{q}_\alpha)$ is underlined by a
  special trivializing atlas $(U_\alpha,q_\alpha)$ of the fiber bundle
  $\pi:E\rightarrow M$, whose trivializing maps are diffeomorphisms
  $q_\alpha:E_\alpha\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \pi^{-1}(U_\alpha)\rightarrow
  E_\alpha^0=U_\alpha\times \mathcal{M}$. This allows us to define smooth maps
  $\varphi^{\alpha}\in \mathcal{C}^\infty(U_\alpha,\mathcal{M})$ such that
  $s_\alpha=q_\alpha^{-1}\circ \mathrm{graph}(\varphi^\alpha)$ as in
  Subsection \ref{subsec:sigmaUfold}:
\begin{equation*}
\varphi^{\alpha}\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \hat{q}_{\alpha}\circ s_{\alpha} = \mathrm{ungraph}(q_\alpha\circ s_\alpha)=p^{0}_{\alpha}\circ q_{\alpha}\circ s_{\alpha}~~.
\end{equation*}
\item As explained in Subsection \ref{spectrivgauge}, the maps
  $\mathbf{q}_\alpha:(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}_\alpha, \boldsymbol{\omega}_\alpha, \mathbf{D}_\alpha,
  \mathbf{J}_\alpha)\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}
  (\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^0_{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\omega}^0_{\alpha}, \mathbf{D}^0_{\alpha},
  \mathbf{J}^0_{\alpha})=(\mathcal{S}^{p_\alpha^0}, \omega^{p_\alpha^0},
  D^{p_\alpha^0}, J^{p_\alpha^0})$ are unbased isomorphisms of
  electromagnetic structures which linearize the diffeomorphisms
  $q_\alpha$. They induce isomorphisms:
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{q}_\alpha^{(s_\alpha)}:(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}_\alpha^{s_\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\omega}_\alpha^{s_\alpha}, \mathbf{D}_\alpha^{s_\alpha},
\mathbf{J}_\alpha^{s_\alpha})\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow}
(\mathcal{S}^{\varphi^{\alpha}}, \omega^{\varphi^{\alpha}}, D^{\varphi^{\alpha}},
J^{\varphi^{\alpha}})\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \mathcal{D}^{\varphi^\alpha}\, ,
\end{equation*}
where we noticed that
$(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^0_{\alpha})^{s_\alpha}=(\mathcal{S}^{p^0_{\alpha}})^{s_\alpha}=\mathcal{S}^{\varphi^\alpha}$ and
we used the fact that the horizontal part of $\mathbf{D}^0_{\alpha}$ is the
trivial flat connection. This allows us to identify $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}_\alpha$ with the
$\mathcal{S}^{\varphi^{\alpha}}$-valued two-form defined on $U_\alpha$
through:
\begin{equation} \mathcal{V}^{\alpha}\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \mathbf{q}_\alpha^{(s_\alpha)}(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}_\alpha)\in \Omega^2(U_\alpha,\mathcal{S}^{\varphi^{\alpha}})\, .
\end{equation}
The relation $J^{\varphi^{\alpha}}\circ
\mathbf{q}_\alpha^{(s_\alpha)}=\mathbf{q}_\alpha^{(s_\alpha)} \circ \mathbf{J}_\alpha^{s_\alpha}$ implies:
\begin{equation} \boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}_\alpha\in \Omega^{2+,s_\alpha}_{g_\alpha, \boldsymbol{\mathcal{S}}^{s_\alpha}_{\alpha},\mathbf{J}^{s_\alpha}_{\alpha}}(U_\alpha)~~\mathrm{iff}~~ \mathcal{V}^{\alpha}\in \Omega^{2+,\varphi^{\alpha}}_{g_{\alpha},\mathcal{S}^{\varphi^{\alpha}},J^{\varphi^{\alpha}}}(U_\alpha)~~
\end{equation}
\end{itemize}
\noindent
The fact that $\mathfrak{C}_\alpha$ is bijective follows immediately
from its definition.  The fact that $\mathfrak{C}_{\alpha}$ induces a
bijection between solution sets follows from the equivalences:
\begin{eqnarray} & \mathcal{E}^{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}_{E}(g_{\alpha},s_{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}_{\alpha}) = 0\Leftrightarrow \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}_{E}(g_{\alpha},\phi^\alpha,\mathcal{V}_\alpha)=0~~,~~\mathcal{E}^{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}_{S}(g_{\alpha},s_{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}_{\alpha}) = 0\Leftrightarrow 
\mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}_{S}(g_{\alpha},\phi^\alpha,\mathcal{V}_\alpha)=0 \nonumber \\ 
& \mathcal{E}^{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}_{K}(g_{\alpha},s_{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}_{\alpha}) = 0\Leftrightarrow \mathcal{E}^{\mathcal{D}}_{K}(g_{\alpha},\phi^\alpha,\mathcal{V}_\alpha)=0~~.
\end{eqnarray}
This follows by a direct but somewhat lengthy computation using
relations \eqref{eomcorresp}, which we will not reproduce here. For
example, it is easy to see that the relation
$\mathrm{d}_{D^{\varphi^{\alpha}}}\circ\mathbf{q}_\alpha^{(s_\alpha)}=\mathbf{q}_\alpha^{(s_\alpha)}\circ\mathrm{d}_{\mathbf{D}^{s_\alpha}}$
implies that the electromagnetic equation
$\mathrm{d}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}^{s_\alpha}}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}}_\alpha=0$ is equivalent with the equation
$\mathrm{d}_{D^{\varphi^{\alpha}}}\mathcal{V}^{\alpha}=0$.

nodes.name: Classical locally-geometric U-fold
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a scalar-electromagnetic structure. A {\em classical
  locally-geometric U-fold} of type $\mathcal{D}$ is a global solution
$(g,s,\boldsymbol{\mathcal{V}})\in \mathrm{Sol}_{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}(M)$ of the equations of motion of a GESM
theory defined by a scalar-electromagnetic bundle $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}$ of type $\mathcal{D}$
with integrable Kaluza-Klein space. We say that a locally-geometric
U-fold is {\em trivial} if the corresponding extended holonomy
group $\mathbb{G}$ is the trivial group.

nodes.name: Scherk-Schwarz construction as a section sigma model
nodes.statement:
Let $M=\mathbb{R}^3\times \mathrm{S}^1$, where $\mathrm{S}^1=\{\sigma=e^{2\pi \mathbf{i}
  \theta}|\theta\in \mathbb{R}\}=\mathrm{U}(1)$ denotes the unit circle and let
$\pi_1:M\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$ and $\pi_2:M\rightarrow \mathrm{S}^1$ be the
canonical projections. Let $1\in \mathrm{S}^1$ be the point which corresponds
to $\theta=0$ and let $g\in \mathrm{Met}_{3,1}(M)$ be a Lorentzian metric of
the form:
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{d} s_g^2=\mathrm{d} s_{g_3}^2+(2\pi)^2R^2\mathrm{d}\theta^2~~,
\end{equation*}
where $g_3$ is a Lorentzian metric on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $R$ is a positive
parameter. In this example, we have $\pi_1(M)\simeq \pi_1(\mathrm{S}^1)\simeq
\mathbb{Z}$. Setting $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2)\in \mathbb{R}^3$, let $C\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \{0\}\times
\mathrm{S}^1\subset M$ be the circle defined inside $M$ by the equation
$x=0$. Orienting $C$ in the direction of decreasing $\theta$ (the
``clockwise'' orientation), its free homotopy class gives a generator
of $\pi_1(M)$.

Given an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$, an
integrable Kaluza-Klein space $(E,h)$ over $(M,g)$ with fibers
isometric to $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ is determined by a morphism of groups
$\rho:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow \mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$, i.e. by an element $U_C\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=}
\rho(1)\in \mathrm{Iso}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ which describes the Ehresmann holonomy of
$E$ along $C$. Let $\pi_E:E\rightarrow M$ be the projection of $E$ and
$U$ be its Ehresmann transport.

Consider the restriction of $E$ to $C$, which has total space $F\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=}
\pi_E^{-1}(C)$ and projection $\pi_F\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \pi_E|_{F}$. For
simplicity, we denote the fiber of $F$ above a point $(0,\sigma)\in C$
by $F_\sigma$. For each point $m=(x,\sigma)\in M$, the Ehresmann
transport along the curve $\gamma_m:[0,1]\rightarrow M$ defined
through $\gamma_m(t)=((1-t)x,\sigma)$ gives an isometry
$U_m:E_m\rightarrow F_\sigma$. These isometries allow us to identify
$E$ with the pull-back bundle $\pi_2^\ast(F)$ by sending any point
$e\in E_m$ to the point $(m,U_m(e))\in \pi_2^\ast(F)_m=\{m\}\times
F_\sigma$.  Moreover, we can identify the fiber $F_1$ with the
Riemannian manifold $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$.

For any $\sigma\in \mathrm{S}^1=\mathrm{U}(1)$, let $\ell_\sigma:[0,1]\rightarrow C$
be the curve in $C$ defined by $\ell_\sigma(t)=(0,e^{\mathbf{i}
  (1-t)\arg(\sigma) })$, where $\arg(\sigma)\in [0,2\pi)$. Notice that
  this ``clockwise''-oriented curve satisfies
  $\ell_\sigma(0)=(0,\sigma)$ and $\ell_\sigma(1)=(0,1)$. The
  concatenation $\ell_\sigma\cdot\gamma_m$ is a curve which connects
  $m$ to the point $(0,1)\in C$. The Ehresmann transport along this
  curve gives an isometry $V_\sigma\circ U_m:E_m\rightarrow F_1$,
  where $V_\sigma:F_\sigma \rightarrow F_1$ is the Ehresmann transport
  along $\ell_\sigma$. Thus sections $s\in \Gamma(\pi_E)$ of $E$
  correspond to maps $\varphi:M\rightarrow F_1=\mathcal{M}$ defined through
  the relation:
\begin{equation} \varphi(x,\sigma)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} (V_\sigma \circ U_m) (s(x,\sigma))~~.
\end{equation}
Recall that $U_C=\rho(1)$ denotes the Ehresmann holonomy of $(E,h)$
around $C$, where $C$ is oriented ``clockwise''. Identifying the free
fundamental group $\pi_1(M)$ with the based first homotopy group
$\pi_1(M,(0,1))$, we have $U_C=\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0^+}
V_{\sigma_\epsilon}$, where for $\epsilon\in (0,1)$ we defined
$\sigma_\epsilon\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} e^{2\pi \mathbf{i} (1-\epsilon)}$. Using this in
\eqref{VU} gives:
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0^+}\varphi(x,\sigma_\epsilon)=(U_C\circ U_m) (s(x,1))=U_C(\varphi(x,1))~~,
\end{equation*}
where noticed that $\varphi(x,1)=U_m (s(x,1))$ since
$V_1=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{M}}$. Thus $\varphi(x,\sigma)$ has a branch cut in $\sigma$
at $\sigma=1$, with monodromy $U_C=\rho(1)$ along
$\mathrm{S}^1$. Accordingly, $\varphi(x,\sigma)$ can be extended to a
multivalued function of $\sigma$ having this monodromy.

The identification \eqref{VU} shows that the section sigma model
defined by $(M,g)$ and $(E,h)$ can be interpreted as a variant of the
ordinary sigma model with source $(M,g)$ and target $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$ which
is obtained by promoting $\varphi$ from an ordinary map to a
multivalued map having monodromy $U_C=\rho(1)$ around
$\mathrm{S}^1$. Mathematically, this is equivalent with an ordinary smooth
map ${\tilde \varphi}:\mathbb{R}^4\rightarrow \mathcal{M}$ defined on the universal
covering space $\mathbb{R}^4$ of $M$ and which satisfies the quasi-periodicity
condition:
\begin{equation} {\tilde \varphi}(x,\theta+1)=U_C({\tilde \varphi}(x,\theta))~~.
\end{equation}
Hence the section sigma model of this simple example gives a geometric
encoding of the Scherk-Schwarz construction applied to the ordinary
sigma model with source $(M,g)$ and target $(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G})$.
nodes.section: 6 A simple example
nodes.statement_short: On M = R^3 x S^1, an integrable Kaluza-Klein space with monodromy U_C turns sections into quasi-periodic maps: the Scherk-Schwarz construction.

This can be identified with a

nodes.statement: 0\longrightarrow V \hookrightarrow T E\stackrel{\beta_\pi}{\longrightarrow} (TM)^\pi\longrightarrow 0\, .

nodes.label: Vseq

nodes.name: Horizontal distribution (general)
nodes.statement:
A {\em horizontal distribution for $\pi$} is a distribution $H\subset
TE$ such that $TE=H\oplus V$; giving such a distribution amounts to
giving a splitting of the sequence \eqref{Vseq}.
nodes.section: A.1 Horizontal distributions and related notions

nodes.name: Set H(pi) of horizontal distributions
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{H}(\pi)$ denote
the set of horizontal distributions for $\pi$.
nodes.section: A.1 Horizontal distributions and related notions

nodes.name: Complementary projectors
nodes.statement:
Given a horizontal
distribution $H$, let $P_V$ and $P_H$ denote the complementary
projectors of $TE$ on $V$ and $H$ and define $X_H\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} P_H X$ and
$X_V\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} P_V X$ for any vector field $X\in \mathcal{X}(E)$.
nodes.section: A.1 Horizontal distributions and related notions

nodes.name: Vertical differential as one-form
nodes.statement:
Notice that $\mathrm{d}^v s$ can also be viewed as a
$V^s$-valued one-form $\widehat{\mathrm{d}^v s} \in{\rm Hom}(TM,V^s)\simeq
\Gamma(M,T^\ast M\otimes V^s)$. When no confusion is possible, we will
denote $\widehat{\mathrm{d}^v s}$ simply by $\mathrm{d}^{v} s$.
nodes.section: A.1 Horizontal distributions and related notions

nodes.name: Vertical tensor field
nodes.statement:
A {\em vertical tensor field defined on $E$} is a section $t\in
\Gamma(E,\otimes^k V^\ast)$, which can also be viewed as an element $t
\in {\rm Hom}(\otimes^k V,\mathbb{R}_E)$, where $\mathbb{R}_E$ denotes the trivial real
line bundle defined on the total space of $E$.
nodes.section: A.1 Horizontal distributions and related notions

nodes.name: Vertical differential pullback
nodes.statement:
The {\em vertical
  differential pullback} of $t$ through a section $s\in \Gamma(\pi)$
of $\pi$ is the tensor field defined on $M$ through:
\begin{equation*}
s^\ast_v(t)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} t^s\circ (\otimes^k \widehat{\mathrm{d}^v s})\in {\rm Hom}(\otimes^k TM, \mathbb{R}_M)\simeq \Gamma(M,\otimes^k T^\ast M)\, ,
\end{equation*}
where we noticed that $\mathbb{R}_E^s=\mathbb{R}_M$.
nodes.section: A.1 Horizontal distributions and related notions

nodes.name: Vertical and horizontal connections
nodes.statement:
Any connection $
abla$ on $T E$ induces connections
$
abla^V=P_V\circ 
abla$ on $V$ and $
abla^H=P^H\circ 
abla$ on
$H$, called the {\em vertical and horizontal connections} induced by
$
abla$ relative to $H$.
nodes.section: A.1 Horizontal distributions and related notions

nodes.name: Vertically non-degenerate metric
nodes.statement:
A pseudo-Riemannian metric $h$ on $E$ is called {\em vertically
non-degenerate with respect to $\pi$} if its restriction $h_V$ to $V$
is non-degenerate.
nodes.section: A.2 Vertically non-degenerate metrics

nodes.name: Horizontal distribution determined by pi and h
nodes.statement:
Then the bundle $H(h)$ of tangent vectors to $E$
which are $h$-orthogonal to $V$ is a complement of $V$ inside $TE$:
\begin{equation*}
TE=V \oplus H(h)
\end{equation*}
called the {\em horizontal distribution determined by $\pi$ and
$h$}.
nodes.section: A.2 Vertically non-degenerate metrics

nodes.name: Vertical first and second fundamental forms
nodes.statement:
The {\em vertical first fundamental form of a section $s\in
   \Gamma(\pi)$} is the symmetric $2$-tensor field $s^\ast_v(h_V)\in
 \Gamma(M,\mathrm{Sym}^2(T^\ast M))$:
\begin{equation*}
s^\ast_v(h_V)(X,Y)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} h_V((\mathrm{d}^v s)(X),(\mathrm{d}^v s)(Y))\, , \quad \forall\, X,Y\in \mathcal{X}(M)\, .
\end{equation*}
Given a metric $g$ on $M$, the {\em vertical second fundamental form}
of $s$ is the tensor field $\mathfrak{S}^v(s)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \nabla
\widehat{\mathrm{d}^v s}$, where $\nabla$ is the connection induced on the
bundle $T^\ast M\otimes V^s$ by the Levi-Civita connection of $(M,g)$
and by the $s$-pullback of $\nabla^V$, while $\mathrm{d}^v s$ is the vertical
differential of $s$ relative to the horizontal distribution $H(h)$.
nodes.section: A.2 Vertically non-degenerate metrics

nodes.name: Vertical second fundamental form need not be symmetric
nodes.statement:
Notice that $\mathfrak{S}^v(s)$ need not be symmetric (even when $\pi$
is a pseudo-Riemannian submersion with totally geodesic fibers, see
below).
nodes.section: A.2 Vertically non-degenerate metrics

nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence

nodes.name: Metric compatible with pi and g
nodes.statement:
Let $g$ be a pseudo-Riemannian metric on $M$. A pseudo-Riemannian
metric $h$ on $E$ is called {\em compatible with $\pi$ and $g$} if
$\pi$ is a pseudo-Riemannian submersion from $(E,h)$ to $(M,g)$. It is
called {\em compatible with $\pi$} if there exists a pseudo-Riemannian
metric $g$ on $M$ such that $h$ is compatible with $\pi$ and $g$.
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence

nodes.name: Sets of compatible metrics
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathrm{Met}_{\pi, g}(E)$ denote the set of all pseudo-Riemannian metrics
on $E$ which are compatible with $\pi$ and $g$ and $\mathrm{Met}_\pi(E)$
denote the set of all pseudo-Riemannian metrics on $E$ which are
compatible with $\pi$.
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the base metric
nodes.statement:
For any $h\in \mathrm{Met}(E)$ which is vertically
non-degenerate, there exists at most one $g\in \mathrm{Met}(M)$ such that $h$
is compatible with $\pi$ and $g$.
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence
conclusions:
there exists at most one $g\in \mathrm{Met}(M)$ such that $h$
is compatible with $\pi$ and $g$

nodes.name: Proof of uniqueness of the base metric
nodes.statement:
Indeed, $g$ is determined by $\pi$
and $h$ through the relation:
\begin{equation*}
g(X,Y)=h(\overline{X},\overline{Y})~~,~~\forall X,Y\in \mathcal{X}(M)~~,
\end{equation*}
where $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$ denote the horizontal lifts of
$X$ and $Y$ relative to $H(h)$.
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence
nodes.statement_short: g is recovered as h evaluated on horizontal lifts.

nodes.name: Met(V)
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathrm{Met}(V)$
denote the set of pseudo-Riemannian metrics on $V$.
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence

nodes.name: Kaluza-Klein metric determined by g, h, H
nodes.statement:
Let $g\in \mathrm{Met}(M)$ be a pseudo-Riemannian metric on $M$,
$\mathfrak{h}\in \mathrm{Met}(V)$ be a pseudo-Riemannian metric on $V$ and
$H\in \mathcal{H}(\pi)$ be a horizontal distribution for $\pi$. The {\em
Kaluza-Klein metric} determined by $g$, $\mathfrak{h}$ and $H$ is the
pseudo-Riemannian metric on $E$ defined through:
\begin{equation} h_{g, \mathfrak{h}, H}(X,Y)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \mathfrak{h}(X_V,Y_V)+g^\pi( (\mathrm{d} \pi)_H
(X_H),(\mathrm{d} \pi)_H(Y_H))\, , \quad \forall\, X,Y\in \mathcal{X}(E)\, .
\end{equation}
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence

nodes.name: Kaluza-Klein metric formula
nodes.statement:
h_{g, \mathfrak{h}, H}(X,Y)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \mathfrak{h}(X_V,Y_V)+g^\pi( (\mathrm{d} \pi)_H
(X_H),(\mathrm{d} \pi)_H(Y_H))\, , \quad \forall\, X,Y\in \mathcal{X}(E)\, .
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence
nodes.label: KK

nodes.name: Proof that Kaluza-Klein metrics are compatible
nodes.statement:
Notice that $h_{g,\mathfrak{h},H}|_{V}=\mathfrak{h}$, so the Kaluza-Klein metric is
vertically non-degenerate with respect to $\pi$. Moreover, we have
$h_{g,\mathfrak{h},H}|_H=g^\pi\circ ((\mathrm{d}\pi)_H\otimes (\mathrm{d}\pi)_H)$, hence
$(\mathrm{d} \pi)_H$ is an isometry between the pseudo-Euclidean
distributions $(H, h_{g,\mathfrak{h},h}|_H)$ and $((TM)^\pi, g^\pi)$.
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence
nodes.statement_short: Check vertical non-degeneracy and that (dpi)_H is an isometry.

nodes.name: Kaluza-Klein metrics are compatible
nodes.statement:
Thus the
Kaluza-Klein metric is compatible with $\pi$ and $g$, i.e. we have
$h_{g,\mathfrak{h},H}\in \mathrm{Met}_{\pi,g}(E)\subset \mathrm{Met}_\pi(E)$.
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence
conclusions:
the
Kaluza-Klein metric is compatible with $\pi$ and $g$

nodes.name: Characterization of compatible metrics
nodes.statement:
Let $h$ be a pseudo-Riemannian metric on $E$ and $g$ be a
pseudo-Riemannian metric on $M$. Then the following statements are
equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[1.]
\item $h$ is compatible with $\pi$ and $g$, i.e. we have $h\in
  \mathrm{Met}_{\pi,g}(E)$.
\item $h$ is vertically non-degenerate with respect to $\pi$ and
  coincides with the Kaluza-Klein metric determined by $H\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} H(h)$,
  $g$ and by the metric $h_V\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} h|_{V}\in \mathrm{Met}(V)$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, $h$ is uniquely determined by $H(h)$, $g$ and $h_V$.

nodes.name: Kaluza-Klein correspondence is bijective
nodes.statement:
For every $g\in \mathrm{Met}(M)$, the map $\mathcal{K}_\pi(g,\cdot,
\cdot):\mathrm{Met}(V)\times \mathcal{H}(\pi)\rightarrow \mathrm{Met}_{\pi,g}(E)$ is
bijective. In particular, the Kaluza-Klein correspondence
$\mathcal{K}_\pi$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{Met}(M)\times\mathrm{Met}(V)\times
\mathcal{H}(\pi)$ to $\mathrm{Met}_\pi(E)$.

nodes.name: Signature of Kaluza-Klein metrics
nodes.statement:
If $g\in \mathrm{Met}(M)$ has signature $(p,q)$ and $\mathfrak{h}\in \mathrm{Met}(V)$ has
signature $(p_V,q_V)$, then the Kaluza-Klein metric
$h=\mathcal{K}_\pi(g,\mathfrak{h},H)$ determined by $g$, $\mathfrak{h}$ and any
horizontal distribution $H$ has signature $(p+p_V,q+q_V)$.
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence
conclusions: has signature $(p+p_V,q+q_V)$

nodes.name: Lorentzian Kaluza-Klein correspondence
nodes.statement:
The restriction of the Kaluza-Klein
correspondence gives a bijection:
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{K}_\pi:\mathrm{Met}_{d-1,1}(M)\times \mathrm{Met}_{n,0}(V)\times \mathcal{H}(\pi)\stackrel{\sim}{\rightarrow} \mathrm{Met}^{d+n-1,1}_\pi(E)\, ,
\end{equation*}
where $\mathrm{Met}^{d+n-1,1}_\pi(g)\stackrel{{\rm def.}}{=} \mathrm{Met}_\pi(E)\cap \mathrm{Met}_{d+n-1,1}(E)$
is the set of all Lorentzian metrics on $E$ which are compatible with
$\pi$.
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence
conclusions:
The restriction of the Kaluza-Klein
correspondence gives a bijection

nodes.name: Lorentzian submersion (appendix)
nodes.statement:
A {\em Lorentzian submersion} from $(E,h)$ to $(M,g)$ is a surjective
pseudo-Riemannian submersion from $(E,h)$ to $(M,g)$, where $(E,h)$
and $(M,g)$ are Lorentzian manifolds.

nodes.name: Lorentzian submersions parameterized by vertical metrics and horizontal distributions
nodes.statement:
The remarks above show that the set of Lorentzian metrics $h$ on $E$
for which $\pi:(E,h)\rightarrow (M,g)$ is a Lorentzian submersion is
in bijection with the set $\mathrm{Met}_{d,0}(V)\times \mathcal{H}(\pi)$ through the
Kaluza-Klein correspondence.
nodes.section: A.3 The Kaluza-Klein correspondence
conclusions: in bijection with the set $\mathrm{Met}_{d,0}(V)\times \mathcal{H}(\pi)$

nodes.name: Proof of local equivalence in the integrable case
nodes.statement:
A simple particular case arises when $H|_W$ is Frobenius
integrable. In this situation, one can find adapted coordinates
$(W,u,y)$ such that $H$ identifies locally with the integrable
distribution $H=(TM)^\pi$ (which is spanned by
$\frac{\partial}{\partial u^0}\ldots \frac{\partial}{\partial u^3}$)
and such that $\frac{\partial}{\partial u^\mu}$ are invariant under
the Ehresmann transport of $H$.  We can then take
$e_\mu=\frac{\partial}{\partial u^\mu}$, which corresponds to
$e_\mu^{~\nu}=\delta_\mu^\nu$ and $e_\mu^{~A}=0$. Thus $f_\mu^A=0$ and
the Kaluza-Klein metric reduces to:
\begin{equation} h=_W g_{\mu\nu}^\pi \mathrm{d} u^\mu\odot \mathrm{d} u^\nu+h_{AB} \mathrm{d} y^A \odot \mathrm{d} y^B~~.
\end{equation}
Since $h_{V}$ is invariant under Ehresmann transport (which proceeds
through isometries of the fibers) the coefficients $h_{AB}$ are
independent of $x$ and coincide with the metric coefficients of the
fiber:
\begin{equation} h_{AB}=\mathcal{G}_{AB}(y)~~.
\end{equation}
Hence the metric \eqref{h0} reduces to the product metric $g\times
\mathcal{G}$. We have $\Gamma_{\mu A}^C=0$, hence the coefficients
\eqref{tauvlocal} of the vertical tension field reduce to the local
form of an ordinary sigma model:
\begin{equation*}
\tau^v(s)^C=\partial^\mu\partial_\mu \varphi^C+\Gamma^C_{AB}\partial_\mu\varphi^A\partial^\mu\varphi^B - 
g^{\mu\nu}K_{\mu\nu}^\rho \partial_\rho\varphi^C
\end{equation*}
On the other hand, the restriction of $\mathbf{\Phi}$ to $W$ is a function:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{\Phi}|_{W}\colon W\to \mathbb{R}\, ,
\end{equation}
which in principle depends both on $u^{\mu}$ and $y^{A}$. 
Equation \eqref{Vvert} implies:
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{d}\mathbf{\Phi}|_{W} = \frac{\partial}{\partial u^{\mu}} \mathbf{\Phi}|_{W}\, \mathrm{d} u^{\mu} + 
\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{A}} \mathbf{\Phi}|_{W}\, \mathrm{d} y^{A}= \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{A}} \mathbf{\Phi}|_{W} - f^{~A}_{\nu}\frac{\partial}{\partial y^{A}} \mathbf{\Phi}|_{W}\right)\, \mathrm{d} y^A\, .
\end{equation}  
Since integrability of $H|_W$ implies $f^{A}_{\mu} = 0$ (see above), we
find that $\mathbf{\Phi}|_W$ only depends on $y^{A}$:
\begin{equation}
\frac{\partial}{\partial u^{\mu}} \mathbf{\Phi}|_{W} = 0\, , \quad \mathrm{d}\mathbf{\Phi}|_{W} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{A}} \mathbf{\Phi}|_{W}\, \mathrm{d} y^A\, . 
\end{equation}
Thus $\mathbf{\Phi}|_W(x,y)=\Phi_W(y)$ for some function $\Phi_W$.

\end{eqnarray}

\mathbf{q}^{s}_{\alpha}(e^{s}_{M})$ form a flat symplectic frame $\mathcal{E}^\alpha$
of $\mathcal{S}^{\varphi^\alpha}$.
